I remember the poet Tom Paulin on The Late Review, which was a late night show that did cultural criticism - books, arts, movies etc - from a highbrow perspective, so they would have talented writers and smart critics like Paulin on, and also Tony Parsons. Pratchett was featured on the show because he was selling a lot of books at the time, and so TLR I guess felt they needed to acknowledge this phenomenon despite the fact they didn’t usually do SFF because those genres were considered unserious and unliterary. And at one point, dismissing Pratchett witheringly, Paulin said ‘he doesn’t even write in chapters’. This sent me to the shelves to check, as I hadn’t ever noticed this. What you do notice when you check is that Pratchett’s sections are pretty short for chapters - you would either need a lot of chapters or they’d need to be quite arbitrarily divided up.

Answer: Let us first consider one of my favourite recognisable London graffiti artists, and then the worst one, and then we’ll get to Banksy. This is HELCH: What I like about Helch is the pleasing typography and the cheerful, bold expression of it. It makes me smile whenever I turn a corner and spot one in some otherwise brown and dilapidated lot. It just feels decorative and playful? Here’s London’s worst graffiti artist, Dr Hokes: I’m not going to bother with more examples because that’s the only thing he can draw, a doctor in full PPE gear. Obviously, from a technical point of view, it’s shit, but what’s worse is that this guy is a ‘plandemic’ crank who thinks covid was a hoax. And this stuff went up during the pandemic when friends of mine were dressed like this every day trying to keep people alive. The terrible political message compounds the incompetence of the art. I scowl whenever I see one, which is quite a lot because he’s very prolific. There isn’t any sense of judiciously decorating the built environment, which is what I think gives Helch and all good graffiti artists a note of grace. Helch thinks about where the tag goes and where it would look best. Hokes appears to slap this tag everywhere he can, presumably because his main motivation is to proselytise. (A recent tag was annotated with the advice to watch Andrew Bridgen on YouTube.) What both artists have in common is that their output is very similar each time - Helch’s HELCH or H, Hokes’ dismal caricature. Banksy, on the other hand, is doing something different each time. Like Helch, he’s interacting with the built environment. Banksy often chooses to incorporate his work into the ‘canvas’: Like Hokes, he’s generally intending to make more of a statement than just fun typography, or often, jokes. This is essentially a cartoon, for laffs: Here’s a joke (?) with more edge: ‘Valentine’s Day Mascara’: a battered woman disposes of her abusive husband. The jokelike quality of it is expressed in the comedic exaggeration of the way the 50s housewife is painted, and the slapstick of the corpse’s feet protruding from the freezer. But the violence is unsettling, isn’t it. Banksy’s most recent series of works is the London Zoo collection, which includes the elephants above, and you can see the same sort of stuff going around. The playful interaction of paint, bricks and mortar: It’s tied together by the mural on the entrance to the Zoo, which repeats another Banksy trope, the wall being lifted up or breached: So: do I reckon Banksy’s art is any good? I think it is technically very well executed. The stencils (I assume they are generally stencils) are nicely made. That rhino is excellent. The housewife in VDM is very good, the flat graphic print on her dress and her magazine-ad posture particularly. I think they improve the environment. The blank shutter of London Zoo is better for having some well-executed art on it, rather than, say, Dr Hokes, who has daubed another of his crappy PPE men just down the road on a different building. I enjoy seeing a Banksy much as I enjoy seeing a Helch. Let’s check in with his representatives about the Zoo series: “The artist’s vision is simple: the latest street art has been designed to cheer up the public during a period when the news headlines have been bleak, and light has often been harder to spot than shade.” Fair enough. When he is making a point beyond cheering you up, I don’t think that Banksy has a great deal that is super interesting to say. I mean, I like his cartoon jokes, that’s just good clean fun, if not Great Art. But beyond that he’s often doing stuff which I think is a bit trite: Here we have a little girl frisking a soldier. It is I guess saying that a world in which soldiers have to defer to the authority of little girls is better than the converse of that. It’s a simple reversal. It’s not doing much for me. Or here’s his conventional painting Devolved Parliament: Partly this seems an excuse for the punning title, which would make this a joke, but I guess he’s also just doing bathos: our leaders are basically just animals borrowing the pretend dignity of their surroundings? I dunno, again, not really feeling it. If you look at the Zoo series again and you reframed it not as the work of a rebellious graffiti artist but as a viral marketing campaign commisioned by the Zoological Society of London, it doesn’t really seem that different? I mean: I have met a lot of graphic designers and other creatives who could conceptualise and execute this. The concept isn’t stunningly creative: we pretend that animals have escaped from the Zoo and are frolicking in the city in various ways. The art is good but not stunningly so. It doesn’t take a creative artistic genius to produce this work; a couple of smart professionals could have done so as part of their day jobs. So: Banksy any good? I think he’s a good, successful, commercial artist. I don’t think he’s stunning, outstanding, or a genius. Lastly, I’m going to just note my favourite work of his, which isn’t a mural or a painting but is in fact a designed object, a piece of clothing: The Union Jack-emblazoned stab vest Stormzy wore at Glastonbury. That, I thought, was genuinely interesting and thought-provoking, at least a couple of layers deep.

Question: Literary agent recommendation? I have 0 idea how that works, does anyone know any literary agents who treat you like a client and not just take most of your money? Where to even start looking? Most publishing companies won't take submissions without
Answer: Reputable literary agents (rather than scam artists) don’t charge you for representation. They make their money on commission, taking typically 15% of your advances/royalties. This means that in order to make any money, they have to sell your book to a publisher. This in turn means that a good place to start looking for a literary agent is in a bookshop, because almost all the books you’ll find there have been sold by an agent, and you want an agent who can in fact sell books. (Scam artists do not need to sell books because they get their money from authors). First, identify where your book will sell. What are the books that are like it, in that ‘if you liked X, you’ll like Y’ way? What shelf would it sit on in a bookshop? Which category on Amazon? Make a list of the books that would be your book’s neighbours and look up their authors online. It should be fairly easy to find out who represents them. Look them up. See if they’re open for submissions. If so, follow the submission guidelines closely. Don’t get involved with anyone who either wants money from you, or (this is another common scam) wants you to go and pay for editorial services offered by some business they recommend. This is generally just them in a false moustache, or a kickback scheme.

Question: Why are they using a blue screen instead of green nowadays in movie shoots?
Answer: They still use both. If you’re shooting a scene with a lot of green objects in the shot you’ll want to use the blue screen, and vice versa. They’re interchangeable to an extent, because the main point is just to use colours which don’t tend to show up in human skin tones. One difference is that green is brighter than blue - a luminous green is easier for a digital camera to pick up - but it does mean that the lighting of the scene changes. If you’re shooting a night scene against a luminous green background, some of that colour is going to spill onto the performers. Better to use the blue screen for that. On the other hand if it’s a bright daytime shot, better to go with green.

Question: I just published a book on Amazon titled "London Fog Murders: A Detective’s Hunt Through The Mist." How do I get sales for it?
Answer: Listen, some of this is going to sound harsh but I think there are some issues you need to address. Please don’t take this as some sort of attack; it’s intended to be a useful answer to your question. Essentially, I think if someone dips into the sample they’re going to fail to be gripped. It is difficult to get spotted in the sea of books on Amazon. It is harder still to get people to click through to the store page. It is even harder to get them to read a sample. Your sample has to be better-written, more intriguing, and more involving than this, or even after you have cleared the first couple of hurdles you are unlikely to make a sale. Intriguing: show us clues. Present a mystery beyond ‘nobody knows why these dissimilar people died’. If this was called ‘The Architect Murders’ and all the victims were architects, we could be thinking ‘I wonder why that is, what could the motive be. Perhaps it is architecture related.’ There is nothing to chew on here. Involving: show us some sort of a real place and time. Show us people. Give us atmosphere. Describe things, in detail, as and when a character’s attention falls on them. Have good reasons for this, but direct the scene. Pick shots. Frame them. Decide what to show and what not to. Decide how characters feel about things. Build their reactions in by description or dialogue. Put us in someone’s shoes, or on their shoulder.

Answer: The current rule is, as far as I know, that if any part of your head, body or legs (not arms - we are essentially talking about any part of your body that can score a goal) is ahead of the last defender, you’re in an offside position. This seems like the version that gives maximal benefit to the defence. The rule that Arsene Wenger is suggesting is that if any part of your body that can score a goal is level with or behind the last defender, you’re onside. Basically, you’d only be offside if there were clear daylight between you. This feels like it gives maximal benefit to the attacker. I recall Jamie Carragher rubbishing this saying that it would cause defenders to be much more conservative, and that, besides, more goals are being scored than ever before. I guess the question is, do we want to see more goals? Because that’s likely what the Wenger plan would lead to. Generally I think the history of football has been traveling in this direction. Three points for a win, the back-pass rule, restrictions on tackles and professional fouls - it’s all been about trying to prevent boring, negative play. But I don’t actually think the current situation promotes negative play, like being able to pass the ball back to the keeper and have her pick it up used to. In fact I think the only real difference between the two proposals in terms of tactics is that it gives a small but significant advantage to attackers for no particular reason. If we want to give attackers even more of an edge, fine, but I don’t think it’s solving a problem, as such.

Question: What can you tell about a publisher's expectations for sales of a book, based on the amount of the advance?
Answer: The publisher will have run a costing which estimates how many books they’re going to sell in the foreseeable future (which is usually a year or two from publication) and how much the royalty income would be from that level of sales. That’s really the basis for what’s an affordable advance level. Of course, if you really really want the book and get into an auction, you’re likely to be pushed higher than that. The proportion of the advance that is above the level you worked out in the costing is called the ‘unearned’, and publishers try to minimise this, but it’s not actually unusual to be carrying an unearned advance on a book. (This is distinct from a book ‘not earning out’ its advance.) In order to work out the sales expectation based on the advance level you will need to estimate certain things that aren’t public knowledge such as the royalty rates payable on the various formats, the retailer discounts, returns rates and so on.

Question: Why does IBM seem to have no voice in the generative AI competition and feels completely absent from this hot competition?
Answer: It’s possible that they have wisely concluded that it’s not actually a good place to be spending their money! People do often say things like ‘ah we’re in the infancy of this technology, it will get much more reliable and powerful’, and I have to wonder how that’s going to happen, because (1) feels like it’s a hardware/energy problem and (2) and (3) would likely require redesigning how it works from the ground up? I’m no expert in this but I feel like they’ve been working on this stuff for a relatively long time now. What we are currently seeing feels a lot like a bubble. Tech companies do have a problem: we’ve got to a point with consumer electronics in particular where it seems like the gains are now extremely incremental, and they’re all basically packed into our phones and tablets. TVs are all now flat HD panels that cost £300. They’re looking for ways to make their new phone somehow exciting. Maybe the screen folds in half, say. Is that actually very exciting? I’m not sure. 3D TVs? 4K? Then it was VR that was supposed to be the next big thing. But again, people weren’t very excited by that. Now they’re stuffing AI into everything, and there’s a vast amount of money washing around without any obvious consumer demand for what it’s being spent on. I think IBM can afford to let their rivals spend billions on trying to make this actually work as a commercial product, right?
